screens.title: Uncompressed Audio: WAV and AIFF
screens.narratorSegment: Uncompressed audio formats store raw sampled data with no reduction. WAV and AIFF are simple containers that keep each sample exactly as recorded, so the audio is a perfect digital clone of the original production master. This means you get maximum fidelity and no compression artifacts, which is why developers keep WAV or AIFF as the authoritative source files. The trade-off is file size: a one-minute stereo clip at 48 kilohertz and 16-bit is roughly ten megabytes. That quickly adds up if you use uncompressed files for hundreds of assets. In practical game work, uncompressed files are ideal for production editing, for very short UI sounds where decode latency must be zero, or for pre-rendered cinematic audio where memory constraints are less important. A common misconception is that larger files always sound better in-game; but if the asset is later transcoded to a lossy format for runtime, the original uncompressed file matters only as the best source for re-encoding. Example: keep your dialog masters as WAV so future encodes start from the highest-quality source. Key takeaway: keep WAV/AIFF for sources and selective runtime needs where fidelity or latency justify the cost. What asset in your current project really requires bit-perfect audio?

keyIdea.text: WAV and AIFF are bit-for-bit replicas of recorded audio; use them as production masters and for latency-critical short sounds.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Uncompressed Audio
Definition

WAV and AIFF

Uncompressed containers storing raw PCM samples with perfect fidelity and the largest file sizes.

Typical use cases
  • Production masters and editing source files
  • Very short, latency-critical UI sounds
  • Pre-rendered cinematic audio where memory is less constrained
Concrete example
A one-minute stereo clip at 48 kHz, 16-bit is about 10 MB as a WAV. Keep these as masters for re-encoding.
Key Takeaway

Use WAV/AIFF as source masters and for a few runtime cases where decode latency must be zero.

Common-mistake
Packing every asset as WAV increases installation and memory costs unnecessarily when most assets can be compressed for runtime.
Pro tip
Keep uncompressed masters in source control; export compressed runtime builds from those masters only once the format decisions are final.
Check your understanding
If a UI click must play immediately on press with zero decode delay, which format family is safest and why?

screens.title: Lossless Compression: FLAC and ALAC
screens.narratorSegment: Lossless compression reduces file size while preserving every original sample. Algorithms such as those used in FLAC and ALAC identify redundancy in the audio stream and store it more efficiently, similar in principle to a ZIP archive. When decompressed, a FLAC file returns a bit-for-bit identical waveform to the original WAV. This makes lossless ideal for cases where absolute fidelity is non-negotiable but some storage savings are still helpful. In game contexts, FLAC might be chosen for high-quality music or important dialogue where you want perfect reproduction without the large footprint of raw WAVs. That said, the savings are moderate—typically 30 to 50 percent—and decompression can require some C P U overhead compared to highly optimized lossy decoders. A common misconception is that lossless is always the best runtime choice for perceived quality. In practice, the larger file sizes and slightly higher C P U load make FLAC less common for short or frequently triggered sounds. Example: a long orchestral track encoded as FLAC keeps pristine detail for archival and QA, while a high-bitrate Ogg might be a better streaming choice in the final build. Takeaway: use lossless when fidelity matters and storage budgets allow.

keyIdea.title: Lossless essence
keyIdea.text: FLAC and ALAC shrink files without discarding audio; choose them when you need exact reproduction but still want some storage savings.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Lossless Compression

FLAC and ALAC

Reduce size without discarding audio data; decompressed audio is bit-for-bit identical to the original.

30–50% typical savings
How it works
  • Find and encode redundant data more efficiently
  • Store metadata and exact reconstruction instructions
  • Decompresses to an exact replica of the original samples
Practical trade-offs
  • Good for archival-quality music and dialog
  • Moderate disk savings but larger than lossy formats
  • Slightly higher CPU decompression vs some lossy decoders
Concrete example
Archive dialog masters as FLAC to save disk space while keeping perfect fidelity for re-encoding or QA.
Common-mistake
Assuming lossless is always best at runtime; larger sizes and CPU cost often make lossy formats more practical for streaming assets.
Key Takeaway
Use lossless when perfect reproduction is needed, especially for archival, QA, or re-encoding workflows.

screens.title: Lossy Compression and Perceptual Coding
screens.narratorSegment: Lossy compression achieves much smaller file sizes by removing audio information deemed less important to human hearing. Codecs such as MP3, Ogg Vorbis, and AAC use perceptual coding to identify content masked by louder sounds or frequencies outside typical listening sensitivity, then discard or heavily compress that content. The key parameter is bitrate: higher bitrates retain more data and sound closer to the original, while lower bitrates produce smaller files with more audible artifacts. For game audio, lossy codecs are often the runtime workhorse because they offer 75 to 90 percent size reductions compared to WAV. Ogg Vorbis is popular in game development for its open-source nature and efficient decoding, while AAC often provides better quality than MP3 at similar bitrates. A concrete example is encoding a music loop at 192–256 kbps for background music to preserve richness, whereas a short environmental loop might be encoded at 128 kbps if disk budget is tight. A typical misconception is that lossy equals poor quality; at the right bitrate, lossy files can be indistinguishable from lossless for many game contexts. The closing question: which assets in your project can accept strategic loss for large storage savings?

keyIdea.text: Lossy codecs discard inaudible data using psychoacoustic models; bitrate controls the balance between size and perceivable quality.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Perceptual Coding
Core Concept

Lossy Compression

Uses psychoacoustic models to reduce data by removing information unlikely to be noticed by listeners.

How it saves space
By exploiting masking and frequency sensitivity, codecs remove or coarsely encode parts of the signal with minimal perceived impact.
Bitrate explained
Bitrate in kilobits per second sets how much data is stored per second of audio. Higher bitrates retain more detail.
Key Takeaway

Lossy codecs offer the best size-to-quality ratio for long assets; choose bitrates based on listening tests in context.

Comparison cards
MP3 — widely supported, good at common bitrates
Ogg Vorbis — open-source, efficient, often preferred in games
AAC — efficient quality vs MP3 at similar bitrates
Common-mistake
Over-compressing critical sounds like voice leads to audible artifacts; always audition in-game context.

screens.title: Quality vs Size: Comparing Formats
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing formats requires looking at three linked variables: file size, perceived quality, and runtime cost. Uncompressed files are largest but cost nothing to decode. Lossless files reduce disk usage by about thirty to fifty percent and restore perfectly at playback, with a modest decompression cost. Lossy formats cut size dramatically—often seventy-five to ninety percent—at the cost of irreversible data loss; however, a well-chosen bitrate can make the loss inaudible for most players. For a concrete comparison, encode the same clip as FLAC, MP3 at 96 kbps and 256 kbps, and Ogg Vorbis at quality settings roughly equivalent. Record the file sizes and listen for differences in clarity, sibilance, and transient response. Another practical axis is C P U: small assets decoded many times per second favor ADPCM or engine-native compressed formats that minimize overhead. A common misconception is to equate bitrate with absolute quality without considering the codec's efficiency—Ogg Vorbis and AAC often sound better than MP3 at the same bitrate. The learning exercise is to build a table of sizes and notes so you can select the best combination for each asset class.

keyIdea.text: Measure size, listen critically, and test CPU cost; the best format balances all three for each asset type.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Quality vs Size

Comparing Typical Settings

A practical table to record file size, quality notes, and CPU cost for each encoding.

Suggested columns for your comparison
  • Format and bitrate/quality setting
  • File size (KB or MB)
  • Perceptual notes: artifacts, clarity, transients
  • Decompression CPU and memory behavior in-engine
Starter table

screens.title: Choosing Formats for Game Assets
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a format is a step-by-step decision, not a single rule. First, ask how critical fidelity is to the player experience: main theme and voiced dialog often demand higher fidelity than UI clicks. Second, consider asset length and repetition: long music tracks benefit most from lossy formats with efficient streaming, while very short sounds may justify ADPCM or even uncompressed storage for zero decode latency. Third, measure C P U and memory: if many assets will be streamed simultaneously, prefer codecs with low decompression cost and small in-memory footprints. Fourth, test in-engine: compressed artifacts sometimes only appear when mixed with other sounds or during dynamic streaming. Example choices: background music — Ogg Vorbis or AAC at 160–256 kbps; dialogue — FLAC for archival, high-bitrate Ogg for runtime streaming; UI sounds — ADPCM or highly compressed Ogg/MP3 at 64–96 kbps. A common trap is treating all assets identically; match format to role. The closing question: for a mobile RPG, which assets would you prioritize for size reduction and which for fidelity? Choosing Formats for Game Assets means assess perceptual importance, asset length, cpu/memory impact, and test results to pick a format per asset type.. In practical terms, decision steps for music, dialogue, ambient loops, and ui sounds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Choosing Formats
Process Flow

Pick a format for each asset type

1. Rate perceptual importance
Decide whether fidelity will be noticed by players in normal gameplay.
2. Consider length and streaming
Long assets favor lossy streaming formats; short assets may use ADPCM or WAV for low latency.
3. Measure runtime cost
Profile decompression CPU and memory to ensure targets meet performance budgets.
4. Test in context
Listen to assets in the engine mixed with other sounds and during streaming conditions.
Quick reference
Music: Ogg/AAC 160–256 kbps. Dialogue: FLAC for masters, high-bitrate Ogg for runtime. UI: ADPCM or 64–96 kbps lossy.
Analogy
Think of each asset as a travel item: some need the full suitcase (uncompressed), others just a carry-on (lossy), and some fit in a pocket (ADPCM).
Key Takeaway

Match format to role: preserve quality where it matters, reduce size where it doesn't.

screens.title: Game-Specific Codecs and Engine Pipelines
screens.narratorSegment: Game engines often include or support platform-optimized codecs designed to minimize runtime C P U and latency while keeping file sizes small. ADPCM is a family of codecs that uses differential prediction to compress audio with very low decode cost. Variants such as IMA ADPCM are popular for short, repetitive effects like footsteps and UI clicks because they decode quickly and keep memory usage low. Console platforms may support proprietary codecs tuned to hardware acceleration, and many engines will transcode your WAV masters into those formats on import. The pipeline typically stores WAV in source control, and the build pipeline produces platform-specific compressed assets to match memory budgets and hardware. A misconception is that these conversions are manual — in modern engines this usually happens automatically, but you must configure quality and target codecs intelligently. Example: configure ADPCM for collections of short sfx so playback latency stays minimal, while letting music be encoded as Ogg or AAC for streaming. Key takeaway: use engine pipelines to generate runtime-friendly codecs from uncompressed masters and check the runtime performance profiles on target hardware.

keyIdea.text: Author in WAV, let the engine transcode to platform codecs like ADPCM or optimized formats for runtime efficiency.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Game Codecs
Architecture

ADPCM and Platform Codecs

Specialized codecs trade a small quality cost for extremely low CPU decompression and small footprint—ideal for frequently played short sounds.

Pipeline pattern
Keep WAV in source control → configure engine import settings → engine transcodes to ADPCM/Ogg/AAC for each platform → runtime uses optimized assets.
Performance note
ADPCM decodes with very low CPU, making it preferable for hundreds of tiny effects; test memory and latency on target hardware.
Concrete example
Footsteps: pack many short samples as ADPCM to keep the active memory footprint small and minimize decode time.
Common-mistake
Assuming platform codecs match desktop behavior. Always profile on the target device because hardware decoders and memory hierarchies differ.
Key Takeaway

Use engine pipelines to generate runtime formats. Choose ADPCM or platform codecs for low-latency, low-CPU short sounds.

screens.narratorSegment: Hands-on conversions make abstract differences concrete. You can use a DAW like Audacity to export to MP3, Ogg, and FLAC, but command-line tools like FFmpeg are fast for batch work. Use a high-quality WAV master at 48 kilohertz and 24-bit if available. Export FLAC to preserve exact data. For lossy testing, encode an MP3 at 96 kbps and 256 kbps to observe differences, and encode Ogg Vorbis at a low and a high quality setting to compare. Example FFmpeg commands are provided so you can reproduce results consistently across assets. A common misconception is that converting an already-compressed lossy file to another lossy format will improve quality—transcoding between lossy formats compounds artifacts. The workflow is: keep WAV masters, export multiple target encodes, record their sizes, and listen in your engine. Try encoding the same clip at two bitrates and compare the size and perceived clarity to internalize how bitrate affects artifacts and size. FFmpeg examples

Run these from the terminal to create consistent encodes from a WAV master. Replace input.wav and output names as needed.

# Convert to MP3 96 kbps
ffmpeg -i input.wav -b:a 96k output_mp3_96.mp3

# Convert to MP3 256 kbps
ffmpeg -i input.wav -b:a 256k output_mp3_256.mp3

# Convert to Ogg Vorbis Quality 3
ffmpeg -i input.wav -q:a 3 output_ogg_q3.ogg

# Convert to Ogg Vorbis Quality 8
ffmpeg -i input.wav -q:a 8 output_ogg_q8.ogg

# Convert to FLAC (lossless)
ffmpeg -i input.wav output_flac.flac

  • Export multiple target encodes for comparison
  • Record file sizes and listening notes
  • Test encodes in-engine under normal playback conditions
Concrete example
Export a 10-second complex clip to FLAC and MP3 96/256, then compare file sizes and note where artifacts appear.
Misconception
Re-encoding lossy-to-lossy does not recover quality; always re-encode from the uncompressed master.

screens.title: Runtime Performance: CPU, Memory, and Latency
screens.narratorSegment: Compression choices directly affect runtime performance across three axes: C P U for decompression, memory for preloaded assets, and latency for short sounds. Uncompressed audio removes decode cost but increases memory use. Lossless decompression costs moderate C P U and still requires buffers in memory. Lossy decoders vary: some efficient codecs decode rapidly with low C P U, while others consume more cycles. ADPCM variants are designed to be extremely cheap to decode, making them ideal for hundreds of short sounds where latency is critical. Streaming large lossy files from disk reduces memory pressure but increases continuous C P U overhead for decoding; preloading uncompressed or less-compressed audio uses more memory but lowers per-play C P U. A common misconception is that higher C P U means worse performance always—what matters is the balance: a slight C P U cost to decode a smaller file frequently streamed can be preferable to holding a huge uncompressed file in memory. Example test: measure memory and C P U while streaming a long music loop as Ogg and compare to a preloaded WAV. The closing question: what are your engine limits for memory and C P U, and how will that change your format choices?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Runtime Performance
Performance

CPU, Memory, Latency

Understand how decode cost, buffering, and streaming choices interact with your engine and target hardware.

Memory vs CPU trade-off
Preloading larger uncompressed assets reduces per-play CPU but increases resident memory usage. Streaming compressed assets saves memory but uses CPU continuously for decoding.
Latency considerations
Short sounds need low decode latency. Engine-native codecs or ADPCM minimize start delay and avoid audible popping.
Concrete test
Stream a 3-minute music loop as Ogg and measure continuous CPU. Then compare to preloaded WAV memory usage and CPU at playback start.
Common-mistake
Assuming mobile devices will tolerate desktop decode costs—profile on target hardware since CPU budgets are smaller on mobile.
Key Takeaway

Profile real assets in your engine to understand the real CPU and memory costs; balance streaming and preloading accordingly.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: A short list of common mistakes and best practices will help you avoid costly errors. First, do not over-compress critical assets. UI and dialog artifacts are distracting, so test those assets at multiple bitrates. Second, do not keep everything as WAV in your runtime build; uncompressed assets inflate installation size and memory. Third, never transcode from one lossy format to another—always re-encode from the WAV master. Fourth, use engine pipelines to generate platform-appropriate codecs and test on target hardware because console and mobile decoders behave differently. Common Mistakes

Over-compressing critical sounds
Lossy artifacts on dialog and UI are noticeable—test and raise bitrate where needed.
Using uncompressed files for everything
This wastes memory and increases installation size with no runtime benefit for many assets.
Transcoding lossy-to-lossy
Quality only degrades; always re-encode from the original WAV master.

  • Identify top 10 assets by memory
  • Run encodes at two bitrates for each
  • Automate engine transcodes

Adopt a repeatable encode-and-test workflow and automate per-platform builds from your WAV masters.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essentials you should remember. First, uncompressed formats like WAV and AIFF give bit-perfect audio and are best kept as production masters or for a few latency-critical runtime cases. Second, lossless formats such as FLAC reduce disk size without discarding data, making them useful for archival and high-fidelity dialog. Third, lossy codecs—MP3, Ogg Vorbis, AAC—use perceptual coding to achieve large size reductions; the bitrate you choose determines the balance between file size and perceived quality. Remember to test encodes in engine context and to avoid re-encoding from lossy files. Finally, use engine pipelines and game-specific codecs like ADPCM for many short, frequently triggered sounds to minimize C P U and latency. These three points guide practical choices throughout a project and help keep both audio quality and performance within budget.

fullNarratorScript:
In game audio, the formats you choose decide whether a soundtrack fits memory budgets, dialog streams without pops, and hundreds of short effects play without raising C P U use. This lesson focuses on three families of formats: uncompressed, lossless compressed, and lossy compressed. You will learn what each family preserves, what it discards, and why that matters when you ship a game. We'll use concrete examples—a one-minute stereo clip at 48 kilohertz and 16-bit, and common bitrates like 96 and 256 kilobits per second—to show how file size and perceptual quality change. You will also see when specialized codecs such as ADPCM are the practical choice for low-latency UI sounds and when FLAC or high-bitrate Ogg Vorbis is best for music or dialogue. By the end of this chapter you will be able to match assets to formats based on installation size, runtime memory, C P U decompression cost, and perceptual importance. As you listen, think about which loss you can tolerate for each asset and which you cannot. That question will guide every format choice you make.

By the end of this chapter you will clearly differentiate uncompressed, lossless, and lossy compression and when to use each. You will be able to identify WAV and AIFF as production masters, recognize FLAC as a lossless option, and name MP3, Ogg Vorbis, and AAC as typical lossy formats. You will also explain how bitrate impacts perceived quality and how decompression affects C P U and memory in a running game. Finally, you will choose the right format for specific assets — music, dialogue, ambient loops, and UI sounds — and understand why game-specific codecs like ADPCM exist for short, latency-sensitive effects. These skills let you design an audio asset pipeline that balances fidelity, file size, and performance. Practice converting a WAV to common compressed formats and compare file sizes and perceived quality to internalize these choices.

In this second objectives slide you'll see the hands-on abilities you'll practice. First, you will convert WAV source files into several target formats and record file sizes so you can quantify the savings. Second, you'll critically listen and note perceptual differences across bitrates to learn where losses become audible. Third, you'll profile decompression costs and memory usage in your engine to observe C P U and streaming behavior. These practical skills let you make objective choices instead of guessing. For example, exporting a 10-second clip as FLAC preserves every sample while reducing disk size by a predictable percent, whereas encoding to a low-bitrate Ogg will drastically reduce size but may introduce audible artifacts. The activity in this chapter pairs conversions with a simple spreadsheet and listening checklist so you can justify each format choice in a production pipeline.

Uncompressed audio formats store raw sampled data with no reduction. WAV and AIFF are simple containers that keep each sample exactly as recorded, so the audio is a perfect digital clone of the original production master. This means you get maximum fidelity and no compression artifacts, which is why developers keep WAV or AIFF as the authoritative source files. The trade-off is file size: a one-minute stereo clip at 48 kilohertz and 16-bit is roughly ten megabytes. That quickly adds up if you use uncompressed files for hundreds of assets. In practical game work, uncompressed files are ideal for production editing, for very short UI sounds where decode latency must be zero, or for pre-rendered cinematic audio where memory constraints are less important. A common misconception is that larger files always sound better in-game; but if the asset is later transcoded to a lossy format for runtime, the original uncompressed file matters only as the best source for re-encoding. Example: keep your dialog masters as WAV so future encodes start from the highest-quality source. Key takeaway: keep WAV/AIFF for sources and selective runtime needs where fidelity or latency justify the cost. What asset in your current project really requires bit-perfect audio?

Lossless compression reduces file size while preserving every original sample. Algorithms such as those used in FLAC and ALAC identify redundancy in the audio stream and store it more efficiently, similar in principle to a ZIP archive. When decompressed, a FLAC file returns a bit-for-bit identical waveform to the original WAV. This makes lossless ideal for cases where absolute fidelity is non-negotiable but some storage savings are still helpful. In game contexts, FLAC might be chosen for high-quality music or important dialogue where you want perfect reproduction without the large footprint of raw WAVs. That said, the savings are moderate—typically 30 to 50 percent—and decompression can require some C P U overhead compared to highly optimized lossy decoders. A common misconception is that lossless is always the best runtime choice for perceived quality. In practice, the larger file sizes and slightly higher C P U load make FLAC less common for short or frequently triggered sounds. Example: a long orchestral track encoded as FLAC keeps pristine detail for archival and QA, while a high-bitrate Ogg might be a better streaming choice in the final build. Takeaway: use lossless when fidelity matters and storage budgets allow.

Lossy compression achieves much smaller file sizes by removing audio information deemed less important to human hearing. Codecs such as MP3, Ogg Vorbis, and AAC use perceptual coding to identify content masked by louder sounds or frequencies outside typical listening sensitivity, then discard or heavily compress that content. The key parameter is bitrate: higher bitrates retain more data and sound closer to the original, while lower bitrates produce smaller files with more audible artifacts. For game audio, lossy codecs are often the runtime workhorse because they offer 75 to 90 percent size reductions compared to WAV. Ogg Vorbis is popular in game development for its open-source nature and efficient decoding, while AAC often provides better quality than MP3 at similar bitrates. A concrete example is encoding a music loop at 192–256 kbps for background music to preserve richness, whereas a short environmental loop might be encoded at 128 kbps if disk budget is tight. A typical misconception is that lossy equals poor quality; at the right bitrate, lossy files can be indistinguishable from lossless for many game contexts. The closing question: which assets in your project can accept strategic loss for large storage savings?

Comparing formats requires looking at three linked variables: file size, perceived quality, and runtime cost. Uncompressed files are largest but cost nothing to decode. Lossless files reduce disk usage by about thirty to fifty percent and restore perfectly at playback, with a modest decompression cost. Lossy formats cut size dramatically—often seventy-five to ninety percent—at the cost of irreversible data loss; however, a well-chosen bitrate can make the loss inaudible for most players. For a concrete comparison, encode the same clip as FLAC, MP3 at 96 kbps and 256 kbps, and Ogg Vorbis at quality settings roughly equivalent. Record the file sizes and listen for differences in clarity, sibilance, and transient response. Another practical axis is C P U: small assets decoded many times per second favor ADPCM or engine-native compressed formats that minimize overhead. A common misconception is to equate bitrate with absolute quality without considering the codec's efficiency—Ogg Vorbis and AAC often sound better than MP3 at the same bitrate. The learning exercise is to build a table of sizes and notes so you can select the best combination for each asset class.

Choosing a format is a step-by-step decision, not a single rule. First, ask how critical fidelity is to the player experience: main theme and voiced dialog often demand higher fidelity than UI clicks. Second, consider asset length and repetition: long music tracks benefit most from lossy formats with efficient streaming, while very short sounds may justify ADPCM or even uncompressed storage for zero decode latency. Third, measure C P U and memory: if many assets will be streamed simultaneously, prefer codecs with low decompression cost and small in-memory footprints. Fourth, test in-engine: compressed artifacts sometimes only appear when mixed with other sounds or during dynamic streaming. A common trap is treating all assets identically; match format to role. The closing question: for a mobile RPG, which assets would you prioritize for size reduction and which for fidelity?
